summary_paragraph: Mr. Johnson, a man with a history of chronic alcohol abuse, atrial fibrillation, and hypertension, was admitted with worsening right upper quadrant abdominal pain radiating to the right lower quadrant and retrosternal chest pain. He had vomited twice and reported a fall four days prior with brief loss of consciousness. In the ED, he was hypotensive with a systolic blood pressure in the 70s, requiring fluid resuscitation. Workup revealed acute kidney injury likely due to prerenal causes, which improved with IV fluids. CT imaging showed mesenteric stranding suggestive of mesenteritis, fatty liver, trace ascites, and bilateral pleural effusions with right predominance. His cardiac evaluation was notable for new T-wave inversions on EKG, but serial troponins were negative. A nuclear stress test revealed normal perfusion but severely reduced ejection fraction of 16%, indicating possible alcohol- or tachycardia-induced cardiomyopathy. He displayed signs of alcohol withdrawal and was managed with CIWA protocol, thiamine, and multivitamins. Despite medical recommendations, he left the hospital against medical advice immediately after completing the stress test, declining further evaluation and discharge instructions.
